title: Push for most, pull for a few
sub: How a hybrid feed handles an ordinary account and a celebrity account.

frames.caption: Ann has three followers, including you. Star has 40 million followers, you among them. Each follower has a precomputed feed (a cached list of post ids).
Ann posts. Push (fan-out on write): a worker writes the post id into each follower's feed. Three writes, done in milliseconds, and reading a feed stays a single lookup.

Star posts. Pushing it would mean 40 million feed writes for one post: minutes of fan-out lag and a burst of load. So accounts above a follower threshold are not fanned out. The post is written once, to Star's own timeline.

You open the app. The feed service reads your precomputed feed (Ann's post) and, at the same moment, pulls recent posts from the few celebrity accounts you follow. It merges the two by time or ranking score.

Each model's worst case is now bounded: no post triggers millions of writes, and no read pulls from more than the handful of celebrities a user follows. Twitter moved to this kind of hybrid after high-follower accounts caused fan-out delays of minutes.
